column3: Scenario
column4: Details
column5: Expected Behaviour

column3: Edit the body text only
column4: Change a paragraph in the article body directly in Prod (not touching Sandbox). Confirms a PR opens with the updated body content in the matching markdown file, and nothing else changes.
column5: A PR opens with only the body content updated in the matching markdown file. Title, url, and all other fields remain unchanged.

column3: Edit the title only
column4: Change the title in Prod, leaving the body untouched. Titles are stored as "[marker] - heading" (see parseTitle in tools/cs-sync/src/lib/entry-content.ts). Confirms the PR preserves the marker and only changes the heading part, rather than mangling the format.
column5: The PR updates only the heading portion of the title, preserving the "[marker] - " prefix intact and unmangled.

column3: Edit the url (rename/move the page's slug)
column4: Change the url field directly in Prod. The script matches which GitHub file to write into by looking up the entry's url. Confirms whether this correctly updates the file at the old path, creates a new one at the new path, or fails to find a match at all.
column5: Because the file is indexed by its existing url, changing the url in Prod means no cs-docs file will match the new url. Expect the lookup to fail to find a match and skip the entry (similar to the "no cs-docs file has url" case), leaving the old file stale rather than renaming or updating it in place.

column3: Edit tags
column4: Add or remove a tag directly in Prod. Tags are explicitly called out in the code comments (entry-content.ts) as real authored data that should count as a change, unlike most other metadata fields. Confirms it actually triggers a PR.
column5: The tag change is treated as real authored content (not bookkeeping) and triggers a PR.

column3: Edit a field outside the synced frontmatter/write list
column4: Edit a custom field on the entry that isn't title, url, description, or one of the api-docs-only fields (api_version, superscript, enable_openapi). Confirms whether the change is silently dropped from the synced markdown rather than erroring, and whether it still triggers a PR that ends up with no visible diff.
column5: Since contentsEqual compares the full entry, the edit is still detected as a change and processed as a direct edit. However, generateFrontmatter never writes that field, so the resulting markdown file has no visible diff. Expect either no PR (git diff finds nothing to commit) or a PR that shows an empty/no-op diff.

column3: Re-publish with no actual content change
column4: Edit a field, publish, then republish the exact same content again with nothing changed. contentsEqual ignores timestamps and other CMA bookkeeping fields. Confirms the second publish is correctly treated as a no-op with no new PR.
column5: Since contentsEqual strips timestamps and CMA bookkeeping fields before comparing, the second publish is treated as unchanged. No new PR opens.

column3: Entry's sandbox-uid tag is missing or stale
column4: Edit an entry directly in Prod that either never carried a sandbox-uid-<uid> tag (never promoted from Sandbox), or carries a stale one from a much earlier promotion. Confirms the comparison against Sandbox still works correctly, since the tag itself is stripped before comparing (entry-content.ts contentsEqual).
column5: The sandbox-uid tag is stripped before comparison, so the Sandbox/Prod content comparison still works correctly regardless of whether the tag is missing or stale.

column3: Matching Sandbox entry is missing or deleted
column4: Edit a Prod entry whose corresponding Sandbox entry either never existed at that url or was later deleted. Confirms this falls through as a genuine direct edit (no Sandbox match found) and opens a PR, per the script's own documented behavior for this case.
column5: No Sandbox match is found, so the edit falls through and is treated as a genuine direct edit, opening a PR, matching the script's documented fallback behavior.

column3: Baseline single simple entry promotion echo
column4: Edit a plain text-only Sandbox entry (no modular blocks/images) and let it auto-promote to Prod. Confirms only the normal Sandbox->GitHub PR appears, and the Prod-side check correctly skips it as an echo with no duplicate PR.
column5: Only the normal Sandbox->GitHub PR appears. The Prod-side pull step recognizes the promoted content as matching Sandbox (an echo) and skips it, opening no duplicate PR.

column3: Batch promotion - several entries at once
column4: Publish a Release containing multiple entries and let all of them promote in one run. Confirms the echo check correctly skips every promoted entry in that batch, not just the first one it checks.
column5: The echo check correctly identifies and skips every promoted entry in the batch, not just the first, so no duplicate PRs are opened for any of them.

column3: Brand-new entry's very first promotion
column4: Create a brand-new entry in Sandbox, publish it, and let it promote for the first time. sb-to-prod.csv Round 1 scenario 6 found Contentstack regenerates a nested _metadata.uid inside modular blocks on creation, which contentsEqual does not strip since it only strips top-level fields. Confirms whether this same bug causes cms-pull-prod to wrongly treat a fresh promotion as a direct Prod edit and open a spurious duplicate PR.
column5: Because contentsEqual only strips top-level fields and Contentstack regenerates a nested _metadata.uid inside modular blocks on creation, expect this mismatch to cause cms-pull-prod to wrongly treat the fresh promotion as a direct Prod edit, opening a spurious duplicate PR.

column3: Sandbox entry's publish_details shape is unresolvable
column4: Find or engineer a case where the Sandbox copy's publish_details can't be parsed into a version (the unresolved flag). Per the code (sandboxMatch && !sandboxMatch.unresolved && contentsEqual(...)), an unresolved match skips the equality check entirely and falls through to sync. Confirms whether this wrongly fires a duplicate PR for a genuine echo.
column5: Per the code's short-circuit logic, an unresolved sandboxMatch skips the contentsEqual check entirely and falls through to sync, so expect this to wrongly fire a duplicate PR even though the entry is a genuine echo.

column3: Sandbox entry unpublished right after promotion, before the pull step runs
column4: Promote an entry, then immediately unpublish it in Sandbox before the pull direct Prod edits step executes (both happen in the same job, but timing within it could still matter). Since the lookup only finds published Sandbox entries, this could show as no Sandbox match and get misclassified as a direct edit even though it was really just promoted.
column5: Since the Sandbox lookup only finds currently-published entries, expect no Sandbox match to be found, causing the just-promoted entry to be misclassified as a direct Prod edit and opening an unwanted PR.

column3: Complex content - JSON RTE / modular blocks with nested arrays
column4: Promote an entry with rich, deeply nested modular block content (tables, images, multiple sections), not just plain text. Confirms the comparison's key-sorting (canonicalize()) correctly treats reordered-but-identical nested content as equal, rather than any serialization quirk causing a false changed result.
column5: canonicalize()'s key-sorting correctly treats reordered-but-identical nested content as equal, so the promotion is recognized as an echo with no false "changed" result and no duplicate PR.

column3: Two Sandbox entries share the same url as the Prod entry
column4: Edge case: if getPublishedEntryByUrl finds more than one Sandbox match for the same url, confirm what happens - does it pick one arbitrarily, treat it as unresolved, or error. A wrong pick here could cause a false-positive echo skip or a false-negative duplicate PR.
column5: Behavior is not clearly defined by the documented logic for this case. It could pick a match arbitrarily, treat it as unresolved, or error. Any of these risks either a false-positive echo skip or a false-negative duplicate PR, so this is a likely gap worth flagging rather than a confirmed-correct path.

column3: Baseline duplicate url across two cs-docs files
column4: Temporarily set two existing cs-docs files to the same url in frontmatter, then edit the corresponding Prod entry. Per getFilePath() in cms-pull-prod.ts, more than one match logs '<N> cs-docs files share url <url>, skipped as ambiguous' and returns null. Confirms neither file is touched and no PR opens.
column5: getFilePath() logs '<N> cs-docs files share url <url>, skipped as ambiguous' and returns null. Neither file is touched and no PR opens.

column3: Duplicate resolves itself on a later run
column4: After scenario 16, fix one of the two duplicate files so only one carries the url, then trigger the next run without changing the Prod entry again. Confirms the next poll now finds a single unambiguous match and syncs normally, rather than staying stuck skipping forever.
column5: The next poll finds a single unambiguous match and syncs normally. The entry is not permanently stuck skipping.

column3: Duplicate url across files in different folders
column4: Set the same url on two cs-docs files that live in different nested folders (not side by side), then edit the corresponding Prod entry. Confirms the ambiguity check catches duplicates regardless of folder depth, since it scans the whole doc index rather than one directory.
column5: The ambiguity check scans the whole doc index, so it catches the duplicate regardless of folder depth and skips as ambiguous, same as scenario 16.

column3: Baseline race - Sandbox edit published right as the scheduled run fires
column4: Publish a Sandbox edit timed to land right as the 5-minute cron tick fires. Since promote and pull run as two steps in one job (see sandbox-auto-promote-csdocs.yml comments), promotion should always complete before the Prod-pull comparison runs. Confirms the edit is classified as an echo, not a direct edit, with no stale-content PR.
column5: Because promote and pull run sequentially as two steps in the same job, promotion completes before the Prod-pull comparison runs. The edit is classified as an echo, not a direct edit, with no stale-content PR.

column3: Promotion step fails or errors before the pull step runs
column4: Simulate or wait for a run where the promote step fails partway (e.g. a transient API error). Confirms whether the pull step still executes afterward and, if so, whether it misclassifies not-yet-promoted Sandbox content as a direct Prod edit since promotion never actually caught up.
column5: If the pull step still runs after a failed promote step, expect it to misclassify the not-yet-promoted Sandbox content as a direct Prod edit, since promotion never caught up, likely opening an unwanted PR.

column3: Manual workflow_dispatch overlapping a scheduled tick
column4: Manually trigger the promote-and-pull workflow at nearly the same moment a scheduled tick is due. Per the shared concurrency group (sandbox-to-prod-promote-csdocs), confirms the second run queues rather than running concurrently, so the pull step never reads a half-finished promotion from the other run.
column5: The shared concurrency group (sandbox-to-prod-promote-csdocs) causes the second run to queue rather than run concurrently, so the pull step never reads a half-finished promotion from the other run.

column3: Baseline unpublish directly in Production
column4: Unpublish an entry directly in Prod (an entry that was never edited via GitHub/Sandbox first, or one already synced). Per current code, cms-pull-prod.ts only iterates currently-published entries with no comparison against a previous run, so an unpublish simply makes the entry disappear from the list. Confirms no PR opens, no warning is logged, and the existing GitHub file is left in place unchanged (now stale).
column5: Since the script only iterates currently-published entries with no memory of a previous run, the unpublished entry simply disappears from the list. No PR opens, no warning is logged, and the existing GitHub file is left in place, now silently stale.

column3: Delete the entry entirely in Production (not just unpublish)
column4: Fully delete an entry directly in Prod rather than unpublishing it. Confirms the same gap as scenario 22 applies to hard deletes too - nothing detects it, the GitHub file remains untouched.
column5: Same gap as scenario 22: nothing detects the deletion, and the GitHub file remains untouched and stale.

column3: Republish the same entry after unpublishing in Prod
column4: After scenario 22, republish the same entry in Prod with no other changes, and no changes made to the GitHub file in between. Confirms the entry reappears in the published list on the next run and is compared/synced normally again, with no leftover bad state from having been temporarily unpublished.
column5: The entry reappears in the published list on the next run and is compared/synced normally, with no leftover bad state from the temporary unpublish.

column3: Edit a custom field only - not title/url/description/api fields
column4: Edit a field on a Prod entry that generateFrontmatter() never writes (i.e. not title, url, description, or the api-docs-only api_version/superscript/enable_openapi). Since contentsEqual compares the full entry against Sandbox, this should still be classified as a direct edit and processed, but generateFrontmatter drops the field. Confirms whether a PR opens at all, and if so, whether its diff shows any visible change.
column5: contentsEqual compares the full entry, so the edit is still classified as a direct edit and processed, but generateFrontmatter drops the field when writing the file. Expect either no PR (no file content actually changes) or a PR whose diff shows no visible change.

column3: Repeated runs after a custom-field-only edit produce no repeat PRs
column4: Following scenario 25, let two more scheduled runs pass with nothing further changed. Confirms the workflow's 'check for changes' git-diff gate correctly finds no file content difference (since the field was never written to disk in the first place) and does not open a new PR on every run.
column5: The workflow's git-diff gate finds no file content difference on subsequent runs, since the field was never written to disk, so no repeat PRs open.

column3: Accented characters and emoji in title or body
column4: Edit a Prod entry's title or body to include accented characters (e.g. café, naïve) and emoji. Confirms the resulting markdown file renders them correctly with no mangling or encoding corruption.
column5: The resulting markdown file renders accented characters and emoji correctly, with no mangling or encoding corruption.

column3: HTML entities and unusual symbols in body
column4: Edit a Prod entry's body to include HTML entities (e.g. curly quotes and ampersands) and unusual symbols (e.g. arrows, degree signs, currency signs). Confirms clean conversion to markdown with no leftover raw entity codes or broken characters.
column5: The body converts cleanly to markdown with no leftover raw HTML entity codes and no broken characters.

column3: Confirm the live Prod environment name matches the code's default
column4: Check the actual environment name in the Contentstack Prod stack UI and confirm it is literally 'production' (lowercase), matching the PROD_ENVIRONMENT default in cms-pull-prod.ts. The code has a comment explicitly flagging this as unverified against the real stack.
column5: The live Prod stack's environment name is literally 'production' (lowercase), matching the code's PROD_ENVIRONMENT default. This is currently an unverified assumption flagged in the code, not a confirmed fact.

column3: Simulate a wrong environment name on a throwaway branch
column4: On a throwaway branch only (never merged to main), temporarily change PROD_ENVIRONMENT to a name that doesn't exist on the stack and run the script via workflow_dispatch scoped to that branch. Confirms whether it fails loudly (preferred) or silently reports zero entries found, matching the pattern already proven for the promotion side in sb-to-prod.csv Round 2 scenario 36.
column5: Based on the pattern already proven on the promotion side, expect the script to silently report zero entries found rather than failing loudly, which would be the less safe of the two possible outcomes.

column3: Entry missing a title
column4: Find or create a published Prod entry with no title field set. Confirms cms-pull-prod.ts logs a warning ('Skipping entry without title/url') and skips it cleanly rather than crashing or writing a malformed file.
column5: The script logs a warning ('Skipping entry without title/url') and skips the entry cleanly, without crashing or writing a malformed file.

column3: Entry missing a url
column4: Find or create a published Prod entry with no url field set. Confirms the same warning-and-skip behavior as scenario 31, and that no file gets written to an incorrect or guessed path.
column5: Same warning-and-skip behavior as scenario 31. No file gets written to an incorrect or guessed path.

column3: Entry missing both title and url
column4: Find or create a published Prod entry missing both fields. Confirms the run still completes cleanly, logging the skip and continuing to process any other entries rather than aborting the whole run.
column5: The run completes cleanly, logging the skip and continuing to process any other entries, rather than aborting the whole run.

column3: Baseline - brand-new entry created directly in Production
column4: Create a brand-new docs_article entry directly in Prod, with a url that has no matching file anywhere in cs-docs/, and publish it. Per getFilePath() in cms-pull-prod.ts, csdocs looks up the file to write into by url via buildDocIndex, and a url with zero matches logs 'no cs-docs file has url <url>, skipped (run nav-apply to create it)'. Confirms this is exactly what happens: no PR, no file created, entry effectively invisible to GitHub.
column5: getFilePath() finds zero url matches in the doc index and logs 'no cs-docs file has url <url>, skipped (run nav-apply to create it)'. No PR opens, no file is created, and the entry is effectively invisible to GitHub until nav-apply is run.

column3: New entry's url differs only by a canonicalization detail
column4: Create a new Prod entry whose url differs from an existing cs-docs file only in a way canonicalizeUrl() is expected to normalize away (e.g. a trailing slash or case difference). Confirms whether it correctly resolves to the existing file (syncs normally) rather than being wrongly treated as having zero matches.
column5: canonicalizeUrl() normalizes away the trailing-slash/case difference, so the entry correctly resolves to the existing file and syncs normally, rather than being wrongly treated as having zero matches.

column3: Gap workaround - create the file via GitHub first
column4: then edit in Prod
column5: Manually add the markdown file in cs-docs/ via a normal GitHub PR first (or run nav-apply per the script's own suggested fix), then make an edit directly in Prod to that same entry. Confirms that once a matching file exists, direct Prod edits sync normally going forward, isolating the gap to the initial creation step only.
column6: Once a matching file exists in cs-docs/, direct Prod edits to that entry sync normally going forward. The gap identified in scenario 34 is isolated to the initial creation step only.

column3: Same scenario on the apidocs stack
column4: Create a brand-new entry directly in Prod on the apidocs stack instead of csdocs. getFilePath() for apidocs builds the path from the entry's content_type and url directly, without checking whether a file already exists (unlike csdocs' url-index lookup). Confirms whether apidocs can actually create a brand-new file straight from a direct Prod entry, which would mean this gap is csdocs-specific, not shared across both stacks.
column5: Since apidocs builds the file path directly from content_type and url without checking for an existing file (unlike csdocs' url-index lookup), expect apidocs to be able to create a brand-new file straight from a direct Prod entry. That would mean the scenario 34 gap is csdocs-specific, not shared across both stacks.

column3: Promoted content is recognized as an echo, not a Prod edit
column4: Promote an entry from Sandbox to Prod and publish it to Production so the pull can see it at all, then run the Detect direct Prod edits step. Confirms the echo guard finally fires.
column5: The entry is skipped as an echo (its content still reproduces the src-hash fingerprint promotion wrote), it is absent from .cms-pull-prod-summary.json, nothing is staged under .prod-sync-staging/, and no PR opens for it. Before the comparison fix this guard never fired for any cs-docs entry, because breadcrumb and the nested block uid always differed.

column3: A genuine Prod edit still opens a PR
column4: On an entry that was previously promoted and is published to Production, edit a paragraph directly in the Prod CMS, then run the pull.
column5: The entry is NOT treated as an echo. It appears in .cms-pull-prod-summary.json under the editor who made the change, and one PR opens for that editor containing the edit. Guards against the comparison fix over-ignoring and swallowing real edits.

column3: A breadcrumb-only cross-stack difference is not an edit
column4: Pick a promoted, Production-published entry and confirm via the management API that its Prod breadcrumb uid differs from its Sandbox breadcrumb uid (they always do, by design). Run the pull without touching either entry.
column5: Skipped as an echo, no PR. The per-stack navigation uid must not read as a human edit.

column3: A nested block _metadata.uid difference is not an edit
column4: Pick a promoted, Production-published entry whose article_content[0].article_section._metadata.uid differs between stacks, confirm the mismatch via the API, then run the pull without touching either entry.
column5: Skipped as an echo, no PR. This nested uid is assigned per stack on create and must not read as a human edit.

column3: The pull runs standalone on the cron and produces no revert PR
column4: Trigger "CS Docs CMS Sync (Prod to GitHub)" via workflow_dispatch while Prod is deliberately behind Sandbox: publish a Sandbox edit to an already-promoted entry and do NOT promote it. This is the exact situation the old promote-then-pull ordering existed to avoid.
column5: The job runs only the detect and open-PRs steps, with no promote step in its step list. The entry is skipped as an echo because Prod still matches the fingerprint promotion last wrote, so no PR opens carrying the older Prod content back over the newer Sandbox change. This is what makes the cron safe now that promotion is manual and may lag by hours rather than five minutes.

column3: Environment name resolves to a UID and entries are actually found
column4: Run PROD_SYNC_DRY_RUN=1 npm run cms-pull-prod and read the two header lines. The old build compared the environment UID against the literal string "production", so it reported 0 entries on every run since the comparison was written, and the failure was invisible because 0 is also what a quiet stack looks like. Partly covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p6, which proves the matcher accepts UID and name form).
column5: Output shows "Environment: production -> bltfe8376c13fe85b9c" with no "(unconfirmed)" suffix, followed by a non-zero published-entry count of roughly 1500. A count of 0, or the word (unconfirmed), is a fail. This is the single most important signal in the whole sheet.

column3: An unknown environment name fails loudly instead of finding nothing
column4: Run with PROD_ENVIRONMENT=nonsense on a throwaway branch. Confirms a misconfiguration cannot masquerade as an empty stack, which is how the original bug hid.
column5: The run fails immediately with a message naming the requested environment and listing the environment names that actually exist on the stack. No files staged, no summary written, no PR.

column3: Entry published to Production and present in the left nav is detected
column4: Pick a docs_article that is published to Production and visible in the left navigation. Change one paragraph of body text, publish to Production, then run the dry run.
column5: The entry is reported as "updated" against the correct existing markdown file, with a fields-modified line reading "body". No other file is touched.

column3: Entry published to Production but absent from the left nav is ignored
column4: Create a new docs_article in Prod with real body content, publish it to Production, and deliberately do NOT add it to the left navigation. Roughly 58 entries in the live stack are in this state already. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p7).
column5: No file is proposed. The "not in nav" counter increases by one. Publishing alone must never be enough to reach the repo, otherwise the sync adds pages no reader can navigate to.

column3: Entry present in the left nav but not published to Production is ignored
column4: Take an entry that is in the nav and publish it to staging or development only, never to Production. Confirms both conditions must hold rather than either one.
column5: Not proposed, and no PR opens. Staging-only content must not leak into the repo.

column3: Entry reachable from the nav only by url slug is detected
column4: Pick a Marketplace app installation guide, edit it and publish to Production. All 54 Marketplace app guides plus roughly 60 other pages are linked by url rather than by entry reference, so a gate that only looked at references would silently exclude every one of them. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p7).
column5: Detected and reported with a nav position under marketplace. Being reported as "not in nav" is a fail.

column3: An unpublished Prod draft is never pulled into a PR
column4: On a published, in-nav entry, type obvious placeholder text such as DO NOT SHIP THIS and save WITHOUT publishing. Run the dry run, then grep the staged output for the placeholder string. The Prod client now resolves each entry to its published version rather than its latest version.
column5: The placeholder text appears nowhere in the staged output. The entry either does not appear at all or appears without the draft text. Remember to delete the draft text afterwards.

column3: A breadcrumb that disagrees with the nav warns but does not reject
column4: Find or create an entry whose breadcrumb names one product while the nav places it under another. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p8).
column5: The entry still syncs, using the nav position, because the nav is what readers actually follow. A warning naming both products is printed and carried into a Warnings section of the PR body so the breadcrumb can be corrected in the CMS.

column3: Two consecutive runs with no CMS activity produce no changes
column4: Run the dry run twice back to back with no publishing in between. Idempotency check. Without it the sync rewrites every published file every five minutes.
column5: Identical counters both times. Created plus updated at or near zero, with the "unchanged" counter holding the large majority of entries. Any change proposed on the second run means the conversion is not stable and the PR must not be merged.

column3: An entry with no article content is skipped rather than written as a title-only file
column4: Find or create a published, in-nav entry whose article_content has no blocks, or whose only block is empty. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p5).
column5: The entry is skipped and counted under "without content". No file is written. Writing a title-only file here is exactly what made every previous PR unmergeable, because it looks like real content and then fails lint for a missing body.

column3: Body content is populated from the article_content blocks
column4: Inspect a staged file under tools/cs-sync/.prod-sync-staging/. The old build read entry.body, a field that does not exist on docs_article, so every file it wrote had a title and nothing else. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p1).
column5: The file contains the full article body: one "## heading" per article_section followed by that section's converted content. A file with frontmatter and no body is a fail.

column3: Description is taken from seo.description
column4: Inspect frontmatter on several staged files. The old build read a top-level entry.description, which does not exist on this content type. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p2).
column5: Every generated file has a non-empty description. An entry whose SEO description is blank falls back to its heading rather than writing an empty string, which would fail the frontmatter schema outright.

column3: The [Marker] prefix is stripped and the title matches the H1 exactly
column4: Inspect a staged file whose CMS title is in the form "[Assets] - My Page". The old build never called the function that splits this, so the raw prefix was baked into every generated file. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p3).
column5: Frontmatter reads title: "My Page" and the body opens with "# My Page". No square-bracket marker anywhere in the file, and the frontmatter title is byte-identical to the H1, which the lint rules require.

column3: A tag-only edit produces a visible file change and opens a PR
column4: Add one authored tag such as qa-test-tag to a published, in-nav entry, change nothing else, and publish to Production. The old build never wrote tags at all, so a tag-only edit produced no file difference and therefore no PR. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (cases p4 and p10).
column5: The entry is reported as "updated" with a fields-modified line reading exactly "tags". The authored tag appears in frontmatter, sorted, so that reordering tags in the CMS does not read as an edit. Remove the test tag afterwards.

column3: No automation tag ever reaches a markdown file
column4: Grep every staged file for src-hash-, sandbox-uid-, pr-, product-, nav-subsection-, and nav-toplevel. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (cases p4 and p22).
column5: None of those values appear in any generated file. src-hash matters most: it is a hash of the entry's own content, so writing it out would make every edit look like a tag change as well, and round-tripping it back to the CMS would corrupt the baseline that promotion's conflict guard depends on.

column3: Rich formatting survives the HTML to markdown conversion
column4: Pick a published, in-nav article containing several sections, a bulleted list, a numbered list, a table, a code block, a Note or Warning callout, at least one image, and both internal and external links. Edit it, publish, then compare the staged file against the page as rendered in the CMS, element by element.
column5: Every element survives: headings as ##, bold and italic, both list types correctly ordered, tables with the right column count, fenced and unescaped code blocks, inline code, callouts as "**Note:**" style lines on their own line rather than merged into the paragraph above, images as ![alt](url) with a working CDN url, internal links relative and external links absolute, and no stray HTML tags anywhere.

column3: Every generated file passes npm run lint with no manual editing
column4: Let the workflow open a real PR and read the lint check attached to it. This is the acceptance bar for the whole rebuild. The old output failed lint three separate ways at once (missing description, missing H1, title and H1 mismatch), and fixing a PR meant a human reconstructing the article body by hand from content the diff never contained.
column5: The lint check is green with no edits to the branch. Any lint error is a fail, and the exact message should be recorded.

column3: List spacing does not trip the double-spaces style rule
column4: Sync an article containing both a bulleted and a numbered list, including a nested list, and read the lint result. The double-spaces rule used to flag every run of two or more spaces anywhere, which meant the "-   item" and "1.  item" forms that the converter emits (and that 13871 existing cs-docs files use) failed lint on every line. The rule was narrowed to prose only. Covered by npm run test:prod-sync (cases p17, p18, p19).
column5: No double-spaces error for list markers, nested-list indentation, or indented continuation paragraphs. Genuine prose double spaces are still caught, including inside a list item, so confirm the rule was narrowed rather than switched off.

column3: Five documents edited by one person in one Release produce ONE PR
column4: As a single CMS user, edit five different Assets articles that are all published and in the nav, add all five to a Release, and deploy that Release to Production in one action. Let the workflow run. This is the headline bundling requirement. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p11).
column5: Exactly one PR opens, titled "CMS Edit detected by <your name>", containing five file changes. Five separate PRs is a fail.

column3: Two different editors in the same window produce two separate PRs
column4: Have two different CMS users each edit and publish one entry inside the same five-minute window. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p12).
column5: Two PRs, each naming its own editor, each on its own branch with a distinct branch name. One combined PR is a fail, and so is a branch-name collision where the second PR silently overwrites the first.

column3: One editor working across several products still gets one PR
column4: As one user, edit and publish one Assets article, one Launch article, and one Administration article. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p13).
column5: One PR containing all three files across three product folders. Bundling is per editor, not per product.

column3: The PR title names the editor
column4: Read the title of a PR opened by a genuine Prod edit. Logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (cases p15 and p20).
column5: Title reads exactly "CMS Edit detected by <editor name>". The name is a real person's name, not a raw blt... uid. A uid means that user is missing from tools/cs-sync/cms-user-index.json and needs adding, because the CMA has no endpoint to resolve an arbitrary user uid with a stack management token.

column3: The PR body reports entry, nav position, change kind, fields modified and time
column4: Read the body of a PR that contains at least one updated page and one newly created page.
column5: A table with columns File, CMS Entry, Nav Position, Change, Fields Modified and Modified At. One row per changed file. Change reads created, updated or deleted. Fields Modified lists only the fields actually changed, and a brand-new page reads "new page" rather than a field list. The origin:prod-sync label is applied and the table is not visually broken.

column3: A lint check run is posted on the PR
column4: Look for a check named lint on the PR head commit.
column5: The lint check is present. Its absence is a fail, because a PR authored with GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger pull_request workflows, so this check is posted explicitly and nothing else will post it. Note that a lint failure deliberately does not block the PR from opening: a red check with the output attached is more useful than no PR at all.

column3: One editor's bundle failing does not cost the other editors their PRs
column4: With two or more bundles pending, make one fail. Deleting that bundle's staged file from tools/cs-sync/.prod-sync-staging/ before running the PR step is the simplest way.
column5: The healthy bundles still get their PRs. The failure is reported per editor and the step exits non-zero only after every other bundle has had its chance. A first failure that aborts the whole run is a fail.

column3: A page created directly in Production lands at its nav-derived path
column4: Create a new article directly in the Prod CMS with real body content, add it to the left navigation under a known section such as Assets then Create and Manage Assets, publish both the entry and the nav node, then run the dry run. This closes the gap recorded in Round 4 scenario 34, where a new Prod entry could not sync because no matching file existed. Filename logic covered by npm run test:prod-sync (case p9).
column5: Proposed as "created" at cs-docs/assets/create-and-manage-assets/<name>.md. The folder chain comes from the nav position and the filename from the url with its first segment dropped. Ask whether that is where a human writer would have put the file, and the answer should be yes.

column3: Unpublishing an entry removes its file in the same PR
column4: Take an entry whose markdown file carries a uid: frontmatter marker, unpublish it from Production, and run the dry run.
column5: Reported as deleted and placed in its own removal bundle. The resulting PR is titled "CMS removal detected: N entries unpublished or removed from nav" and must NOT be titled as somebody's edit, since nobody edited anything. Republishing to Production brings the file back on the next run.

column3: Removing an entry from the left nav removes its file
column4: Leave an entry published to Production but remove it from the left navigation and publish the nav change.
column5: Reported as a removal. Both conditions have to hold for a file to stay in the repo.

column3: A hand-authored file without a uid marker is never removed
column4: Read every path in the proposed removal list and check each one's frontmatter for a uid: line.
column5: Every proposed removal has a uid: marker, which only this sync writes. Any proposed removal of a file without that marker is a stop-everything defect, because it puts hand-authored content at risk.

column3: Exceeding the deletion cap aborts the delete pass
column4: On a run that has at least one removal, run PROD_SYNC_MAX_DELETIONS=0 PROD_SYNC_DRY_RUN=1 npm run cms-pull-prod. Default cap is 10.
column5: A message reading "N file(s) would be deleted, over the limit of 0. Skipping the delete pass" followed by the list it would have removed. Nothing is deleted. If a normal run ever trips this cap, read the list before raising it: a nav reshuffle and a genuine retirement look identical from here.

column3: A partial or failed nav walk aborts the whole run
column4: Force a partial or failed nav fetch, for example by revoking read access on the token or pointing at a stack with no navigation. Without this guard every file on disk would look de-navved and the delete pass would try to remove the entire docs tree.
column5: The run fails with a message about the nav returning fewer than 200 nodes and states explicitly that it is treating this as a failed fetch rather than an empty nav. Nothing is staged and no PR opens. Fix the fetch rather than lowering the floor.

column3: A total API failure cannot cascade into mass deletion
column4: Arrange for no entry at all to resolve successfully during a run that also has removal candidates.
column5: A message reading "file(s) look de-navved but not a single entry resolved this run. Treating that as an API failure and skipping the delete pass". No deletions proceed.

column3: A dry run stages nothing and writes no summary
column4: Delete tools/cs-sync/.prod-sync-staging/ and tools/cs-sync/.cms-pull-prod-summary.json, run with PROD_SYNC_DRY_RUN=1, then check whether either path came back and run git status.
column5: Neither path exists afterwards, git status shows no changes under cs-docs/, and the run ends with "DRY RUN: nothing was staged and no summary was written".

column3: The sync works with no Sandbox credentials at all
column4: Run with both CSDOCS_SANDBOX_STACK_API_KEY and CSDOCS_SANDBOX_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN unset. Sandbox is now optional because echo detection uses the src-hash tag on the Prod entry itself and needs no second stack.
column5: The run completes normally and the promotion-echo counter still reports echoes. A hard failure, or the echo counter dropping to zero, is a fail. Sandbox read access now only sharpens the answer for entries promoted before the src-hash tag existed.

column3: The apidocs stack is refused rather than mishandled
column4: Run with STACK_TYPE=apidocs.
column5: Refused with a message explaining this path is csdocs only, because the nav-membership gate that makes the sync safe has no equivalent in api-docs. Proceeding would be worse than refusing. This supersedes Round 4 scenario 37.

column3: The pull never reads Prod while promotion is writing to it
column4: Trigger the manual Sandbox to Prod promote workflow and the Prod to GitHub workflow at the same moment. They share a concurrency group for exactly this reason.
column5: The two runs serialize rather than overlapping. Both running at once is a fail, because a half-written Prod entry could be read as a human edit.
